568.title: How am I using my soul?
568.word: How am I using my soul?
568.hook: ask often: what am I using my soul for right now? (Meditations 5.11)
568.carry: what am I using it for
568.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes set reminders to ask the question of Meditations 5.11, 'what am I using my soul for right now?', several times a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: back to it. Your line was back to it. After a slip, did you skip the speech and take the next small step? Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Your phone has a battery screen that shows exactly where the power went. Maps, twelve percent. Messages, twenty. That one game, a slightly embarrassing forty. Nobody has a screen like that for attention, or for the inner life. If you did, what would today's breakdown say? Marcus Aurelius didn't have the screen, but he had the question, and he wrote it down as one of the shortest, sharpest checks in his whole notebook. Today: how am I using my soul?
screen: `THE BATTERY SCREEN.` → `WHERE DID THE POWER GO?` → `HOW AM I USING MY SOUL?`

segments.voice: First, the question. What am I using my soul for right now? Marcus writes this in the eleventh entry of book five, and he says to ask it on every occasion. Not once a year at a retreat. Now, and now again. Second, the ruling part. Then he sharpens it. What is going on, he asks, in the part of me they call the ruling part? The Stoics' word was hegemonikon: the steering center of a person, where judgments and choices happen. Marcus wants to check who's at the wheel. Third, whose soul is it? And then the striking part. Whose soul do I have right now? A child's? A teenager's? A tyrant's? A farm animal's? A wild beast's? It's almost funny, and it's very honest. Most of us cycle through several of these in a single day: the child who wants it now, the tyrant who wants it done my way, the grazing animal scrolling for the next bite, the wild animal in traffic. Fourth, why ask often. The question isn't a test you pass. It's a mirror you keep glancing at. Each time you ask, you get a little gap: you notice the tyrant, and the noticing alone loosens his grip. Asked often enough, it becomes a habit of returning, which was yesterday's whole lesson. Here's the plain version for an ordinary day. Three times, stop and ask: what am I using my soul for, right now? You don't have to fix the answer. Just hear it.
screen: `WHAT AM I USING MY SOUL FOR NOW?` · `THE RULING PART: WHO'S STEERING?` · `CHILD, TYRANT, OR WILD BEAST?` · `A MIRROR TO GLANCE AT OFTEN.` · then, large: `WHAT AM I USING IT FOR.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Ask it now: what am I using my soul for, right now? Listen for the honest answer. Maybe it's resting. Maybe it's half here and half in an email. Then ask Marcus's second question, lightly: whose soul is this, at the moment? A child's, impatient? A tyrant's, insisting? Something calmer? Don't judge it. Just name it. Then pick two more times today when you'll ask again. The bell holds the time.
How am I using my soul? Marcus asks it on every occasion: what's happening in my ruling part, and whose soul do I have right now? Today's word.
screen: `HOW AM I USING MY SOUL? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what am I using it for. Ask it three times today, morning, afternoon and evening, and just hear the answer. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

where judgments and choices happen.

trapdoor: what you thought: be mindful.
what it means: check, often, what your soul is being used for and who is steering it.
what a scholar hears: hegemonikon, from hegemon, 'leader', the Stoic seat of judgment and choice; our 'hegemony' comes from the same root.

569.title: The river of being
569.hook: think how fast things pass by, like a river (Meditations 5.23)
569.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes watch moving water and recall Meditations 5.23, letting both worries and successes be seen as part of a constant flow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: how am I using my soul? Your line was what am I using it for. When you asked, whose soul did you find at the wheel? Day five hundred sixty-nine.

Stand on a bridge and look down at a river. It looks like one thing. It has a name on the map. It's been there your whole life. But not one drop under you now was under you a minute ago. The river is real, and it's also never the same twice. More than six hundred years before Marcus Aurelius, a Greek thinker named Heraclitus made that observation famous. Marcus picked it up and turned it on everything, including himself. Today: the river of being.
screen: `A RIVER FROM A BRIDGE.` → `NOT ONE DROP IS THE SAME.` → `THE RIVER OF BEING.`

segments.voice: First, think often. Think often, Marcus writes in the twenty-third entry of book five, how fast the things that are, and the things coming to be, are carried past and out of sight. He doesn't say think once. He wants it to become a habit of seeing. Second, the river. Being itself, he says, is like a river in continual flow. Its activities keep changing, its causes shift in countless ways, and almost nothing stands still. Heraclitus, as Plato reports him, said you could not step into the same river twice. Marcus takes the river and lays it over the whole world: cities, bodies, moods, reputations, problems. Third, the deep on either side. And close beside us, he says, is the boundless gulf of past and future, into which everything vanishes. We met that gulf near the end of book four. Here it's the sea the river runs into. Fourth, so why be swollen up? Then the practical turn. Isn't it foolish, Marcus asks, to be puffed up, or tormented, or upset by these things, as if any of them would trouble us for long? The worry that's flooding you today is water. It's already moving. The pride you feel today is water too. That's the gift of the river picture: it works in both directions. It softens the hard thing, because it will pass. And it keeps the good thing light, so you enjoy it without clutching. You don't have to stop the river. You only have to stop pretending it's a lake.
screen: `THINK OFTEN HOW FAST THINGS PASS.` · `BEING IS LIKE A RIVER.` · `THE GULF ON EITHER SIDE.` · `WHY BE PUFFED UP OR TORMENTED?` · then, large: `THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. If you can, watch flowing water: a stream, a fountain, even a tap running slowly into a sink. If not, picture one. Watch the water move past one point. Each bit arrives, and leaves. Now let one feeling you're carrying today, heavy or light, float into the water. Watch it move past the point, and on. Breathe with the flow. The bell holds the time.
The river of being. Marcus says being is like a river in constant flow: think often how fast things pass, and don't be swollen or tormented by them. Today's word.
Your line: the river. When something feels permanent today, a worry or a win, say: the river, and let it move. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

what it means: see the world as a river, so hard things soften and good things stay light.
what a scholar hears: the river saying is Heraclitus's as Plato reports it in the Cratylus; 'everything flows', panta rhei, is a later summary, not his own words.

570.title: Bad breath
570.hook: angry at someone's bad breath? what can he do, it's his mouth (Meditations 5.28)
570.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes recall Meditations 5.28 with small irritations: either it can't be helped, so let it go, or it can, so mention it kindly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the river of being. Your line was the river. What did you let move past today, a worry or a win? Day five hundred seventy.

Of all the things you might expect in the private notebook of a Roman emperor, a note about body odor is near the bottom of the list. And yet there it is, in the twenty-eighth entry of book five. He doesn't say whether he had anyone in mind. But the picture is vivid: sweaty armpits, bad breath, and Marcus Aurelius, standing close, getting irritated. He used the moment to think something through. It turns out to be one of the most practical entries in the book. Today: bad breath.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S NOTEBOOK.` → `A NOTE ABOUT BODY ODOR.` → `BAD BREATH.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Are you angry with someone whose armpits smell? Marcus asks himself. Angry with someone whose breath is bad? What good will that do you? Second, the plain answer. He has the mouth he has, Marcus says, and the armpits he has. A smell like that has to come from things like that. That's the whole carry: it's his mouth. Most of what annoys us about other people works the same way. The loud chewer. The slow walker. The coworker who says actually before every sentence. These come out of who they are and how they're made, not out of a plan to bother you. Third, but he has reason. Then Marcus imagines an objection. But the man has reason, you'll say; he could notice and fix it. Fine, Marcus replies. You have reason too. So use your reasoning to stir up his. Show him. Tell him, kindly. If he listens, you'll have cured it, and there's no need for anger. Fourth, no drama. And Marcus finishes by saying there's no need for theatrics either. Not the tragic actor, he says, and not the opposite extreme. Just calm, plain dealing. Here's why this tiny entry matters. It breaks every small annoyance into two honest options. Either it's not theirs to change, in which case anger is pointless. Or it is, in which case a kind word works better than anger does. Either way, anger isn't needed. And there's something warm under the joke: Marcus's answer is not to avoid the man, but to help him.
screen: `ANGRY AT BAD BREATH? WHAT GOOD IS IT?` · `HE HAS THE MOUTH HE HAS.` · `YOU HAVE REASON TOO: TELL HIM KINDLY.` · `NO NEED FOR THEATRICS.` · then, large: `IT'S HIS MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small annoyance from someone you see often: a habit, a sound, a way of talking. Feel the little spark of irritation. Then ask Marcus's two questions. Is this something they can change? If not, say quietly: it's his mouth, or her mouth, and let it go. If they can, picture telling them, kindly, once. Either way, notice the anger has nothing left to do. The bell holds the time.
Bad breath. Marcus asks what good anger does at someone's smell: he has the mouth he has. If it can be fixed, tell him kindly. Today's word.
Your line: it's his mouth. Forgive one small annoyance today, or, if it can be changed, mention it once, kindly, without anger. Day five hundred seventy.

571.title: Soon ashes
571.hook: soon you'll be ashes; meanwhile, revere and do good (Meditations 5.33)
571.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes use the plain reminder of Meditations 5.33, 'soon ashes', to clear away small quarrels and do one good act right away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bad breath. Your line was it's his mouth. Which small annoyance did you forgive, or mention kindly, without anger? Day five hundred seventy-one.

Most of us flinch at the word ashes. We keep it at a distance, for funerals and a few solemn days a year. Marcus Aurelius kept it closer. In the thirty-third entry of book five he writes it in the second person, to himself, and very plainly. You'll be ashes soon. Then, in the same breath, he asks what a person should do with the time in between. His answer is short, and it isn't gloomy at all. It's a to-do list. Today: soon ashes.
screen: `WE KEEP THE WORD AT A DISTANCE.` → `MARCUS KEPT IT CLOSE.` → `SOON ASHES.`

segments.voice: First, the fact. Soon, very soon, Marcus writes, you'll be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name. And a name is only a sound and an echo. Second, the squabbling. Then he looks at what people spend their lives fighting over. The things most prized in life, he says, are empty and small: puppies snapping at each other, children quarreling, laughing, and then crying a minute later. He even borrows a phrase from the Greek poet Hesiod, about virtues fleeing the wide earth for Olympus, and applies it to faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth. It's a wry picture of a world that often forgets what matters. Third, so what's holding you here? Marcus asks himself what keeps him attached to any of it, since the things we sense are always changing and our own senses are easily fooled. His answer is to wait calmly for the end, whatever it turns out to be. Fourth, meanwhile. And until then, what's enough? Here's the list. To revere the gods and speak well of them, Marcus says. To do good to people. To bear with them, and to hold back. And to remember that whatever lies outside your own small flesh and breath is not yours and not up to you. Notice the word meanwhile. Marcus doesn't use ashes to stop himself from living. He uses it to clear the desk. The squabbles drop off. What's left fits on a card: reverence, kindness, patience, restraint. For him, reverence meant the gods of Stoic belief. Readers on many paths keep that part in their own words, or in none. The rest is open to anyone: do good, now, while there's a now.
screen: `SOON ASHES, AND A NAME, OR NOT EVEN.` · `PUPPIES SNAPPING, CHILDREN QUARRELING.` · `WHAT HOLDS YOU HERE?` · `MEANWHILE: REVERE, DO GOOD, BEAR.` · then, large: `MEANWHILE, DO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Say the word quietly to yourself: ashes. Let it be plain, not frightening. Now feel your breath, warm and still here. Meanwhile. Bring to mind one good act you could do right now, or within the hour: a message, a kindness, a bit of patience with someone. Small is fine. Decide on it. When the bell ends, do it. The bell holds the time.
Soon ashes. Marcus reminds himself he'll soon be ashes and a name; meanwhile, it's enough to revere, to do good, and to bear with people. Today's word.
Your line: meanwhile, do good. Do one good act now, before anything else on your list. Day five hundred seventy-one.

572.title: The child's top
572.hook: like an old man keeping a child's toy, comfort others without being swept away (Meditations 5.36)
572.howItsDone: People who practice Stoic ethics often describe comforting others warmly while keeping their own judgment about what is truly harmful, rather than either lecturing or catching the panic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: soon ashes, and the job Marcus gives the time in between. Your line was meanwhile, do good. What good thing did you do in the meanwhile? Day five hundred seventy-two.

A four-year-old drops an ice cream cone on the sidewalk. The wail is total. The world has ended. Two grown-ups are standing there. One says, it's only ice cream, stop crying. The other kneels down, says, oh no, your cone, and holds the child until the storm passes. Neither of them thinks the cone was a tragedy. Only one of them was any comfort. Marcus Aurelius, near the end of book five, has a picture for the second grown-up. It's an old man and a child's spinning top.
screen: `THE DROPPED CONE.` → `TWO GROWN-UPS.` → `AN OLD MAN AND A TOP.`

segments.voice: First, the problem. Marcus believes most of what people grieve over isn't truly harmful: money, a post, a reputation. Only acting badly harms the self. That could make a Stoic cold. Someone loses their job, and the Stoic says, that's an indifferent, you're fine. Marcus doesn't want that. In Meditations five, thirty-six, he says: don't be carried away by how things look. Help people as far as you can and as each case deserves, even when what they've lost is one of those indifferent things. But don't imagine the loss is a real harm to them. That's a bad habit of mind. Second, the picture. He says to be like the old man who, when he was leaving, asked for his foster child's top back, remembering all along that it was a top. The old man plays along. He takes the toy seriously because the child does. He just doesn't forget what it is. Third, honesty about the passage. The Greek here is compressed, and the end of this section is partly damaged in the manuscripts. Translators fill the gaps in different ways, and scholars still argue about exactly what the old man is doing. The core is clear enough, though: kindness on the outside, clarity on the inside. Fourth, why it's honest comfort. The old man never lies to the child. He doesn't say the top is worth a fortune. He also doesn't lecture. He meets the child where the child is, and keeps his own head. That's a skill most of us need at a hospital bedside, a breakup, a lost game. Be warm with the sorrow. Stay clear about the size of things, privately.
screen: `MOST LOSSES AREN'T TRUE HARMS.` · `THE OLD MAN AND THE TOP.` · `THE GREEK IS DAMAGED HERE.` · `WARM OUTSIDE, CLEAR INSIDE.` · then, large: `HONEST COMFORT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind someone who is upset right now about something you think is small. A friend's canceled trip. A kid's lost game. A parent's broken phone. Notice the urge to fix it with a fact. Set the fact down. Picture saying instead, oh no, that's hard, and meaning it. Then notice, quietly, that you can still see the size of the thing. Both at once. Stay with that for the sit. The bell holds the time.
The child's top. Marcus's old man treats a toy seriously because the child does, without forgetting it's a toy. Today's word.
Your line: honest comfort. Today, when someone's upset, skip the correction. Say one true, kind sentence about how it feels, and keep your perspective to yourself. Day five hundred seventy-two.

573.title: Cold or warm
573.hook: whether you're cold or warm, sleepy or rested, do your duty (Meditations 6.2)
573.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use 'cold or warm' as a private reminder when they're tired or unappreciated, to do the task in front of them as well as they would on a good day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the child's top, and the old man who took a toy seriously for a child's sake. Your line was honest comfort. Did you get to offer some? Day five hundred seventy-three.

Three in the morning. The baby is crying again, and it's your turn. Or the alarm goes off for the early shift and the room is freezing. Or you promised to help a friend move, and you slept four hours. Every one of us has a list of conditions under which we'd do the thing well. Warm, rested, appreciated, in the mood. Today we open book six of the Meditations, and its second entry crosses that whole list out.
screen: `THREE A.M., YOUR TURN.` → `THE LIST OF CONDITIONS.` → `BOOK SIX OPENS.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's translation, Meditations six, two begins: "Let it make no difference to thee whether thou art cold or warm, if thou art doing thy duty." Then Marcus keeps going, pair by pair. Drowsy or rested. Spoken badly of or praised. Even dying or doing something else. Second, why the pairs. Each one is a condition we use as an excuse. I'll be patient when I've slept. I'll be generous when people notice. Marcus treats all of them as weather. Real, uncomfortable, and not in charge. The job in front of you doesn't change because you're cold. Third, the surprise at the end. He says dying is one of the acts of life too, and in that act, as in any other, it's enough to do well the thing in hand. That's typical Marcus. He doesn't make death a special exam. It's one more task, done as well as you can on the day it comes. Fourth, what he isn't saying. He isn't saying ignore your body or never rest. Elsewhere he admits how much he loves staying in bed. The point is narrower. When the duty is actually yours, right now, the shivering isn't a reason to do it badly. And there's a quiet dignity in work done well while tired. Think of nurses at the end of a double shift, or a parent at three in the morning. Nobody claps. The work is good anyway.
screen: `COLD OR WARM, DO YOUR DUTY.` · `EACH PAIR IS AN EXCUSE.` · `EVEN DYING IS AN ACT OF LIFE.` · `NOT 'NEVER REST.'` · then, large: `COLD OR WARM.`

segments.voice: Settle in. Notice whatever discomfort you have right now: tired eyes, a stiff back, a cold hand, a mind that wants to be elsewhere. Name it plainly. Tired. Cold. Restless. Don't fight it. Then think of one duty waiting for you today that you'd rather do when you feel better. Dishes, a call, a report, a bedtime story. Picture doing it today, as you are, and doing it well. Rest in that picture for the sit. The bell holds the time.
Cold or warm. Marcus's reminder that the duty doesn't wait for perfect conditions, and neither does doing it well. Today's word.
Your line: cold or warm. Pick one duty you're too tired for today, and do it anyway, carefully. Say the line under your breath as you start. Day five hundred seventy-three.

574.title: The best revenge
574.hook: the best revenge is not to become like the one who wronged you (Meditations 6.6)
574.howItsDone: People who draw on Marcus often repeat 'not like them' when someone is rude, as a reminder to answer in their own manner rather than mirroring the other person's.

segments.voice: Yesterday: cold or warm, the duty that doesn't wait for perfect conditions. Did you do one thing well while tired? And today the week closes, so we'll look back too. Day five hundred seventy-four.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, then honks at you. A coworker takes credit in the meeting. A relative says the cutting thing at dinner, the one they always say. And instantly, the reply is ready. Sharper, faster, a little crueler, because they started it. It feels like justice. Marcus Aurelius was an emperor. He could have answered almost any insult with real force. In book six he writes himself one short sentence about revenge, and it fits on a sticky note.
screen: `THE REPLY IS ALREADY LOADED.` → `AN EMPEROR'S OPTIONS.` → `ONE SENTENCE ON REVENGE.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Meditations six, six, in George Long's translation: "The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer." Notice he doesn't say there's no such thing as being wronged. He takes it as given that someone did wrong. The question is what you do next. Second, the trap. When someone is rude and you're rude back, two people have now been rude, and one of them is you. Their behavior has reached inside you and rearranged you. For a Stoic, that's the only real damage they could do. Your money, your reputation, those are outside. Your character is the one thing that's yours, and mirroring them hands it over. Third, why he calls it revenge. Marcus could have said forgive, or rise above it. Instead he uses the word revenge, and keeps it. There's something a little sly in that. He lets the hurt part of you have its wish to win, and then changes what winning means. The wrongdoer wanted you smaller. You stay the size you were. Fourth, the week. Look back at what this week held. How am I using my soul. The river of being. Bad breath, where someone's mouth is just their mouth. Soon ashes, and meanwhile, do good. The child's top. Cold or warm. And now this. Nearly every one of those lines is about the same small room: the space between what happens to you and what you become because of it. Marcus keeps returning to that room, because it's the one place nobody else can enter without your permission.
